prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, bringing atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks, Katori and Ye, and my position has not changed since round 1. Having read all eight statements, the case rests on the criteria I apply to any instrument: a distinct idea (trapping many atoms at the magic wavelength so the light shift cancels on the clock transition), a decisive realisation (Ye's group bringing systematic uncertainty and stability to the 10^-18 regime), and independent reproduction (several national laboratories now run lattice clocks and compare them with agreement far below the caesium standard). That is what turns a record into a result the community believes. The consequences are concrete and lasting: relativistic geodesy at the centimetre scale, tighter limits on drifts of constants and on dark matter, and the basis for redefining the second. No colleague contests the two names, and Danielsson, Eriksson, Mehlig and Olsson each list B025 as an alternative or say they could accept it, so this is the configuration on which a settled judgement is most likely. My proposed wording confines the citation to the lattice clock, which leaves the 2005 comb prize, the 2012 ion-control prize and the Th-229 nuclear clock outside it.
statement.case_against: The serious objection, which Kroll, Lindroth and Johansson state against their own preference, is that this is an enabling measurement capability rather than a new fact about nature, and that it sits next to the 2005 and 2012 prizes. I can answer the overlap point only partly: the comb and the single ion are tools that the lattice clock uses, whereas the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate device concept, but that is a judgement and not a proof. The physics delivered so far is largely bounds and capability, and the strongest discovery-type consequences, such as geodesy and a redefined second, are still in progress. Attribution is not fully closed either. Takamoto's Sr demonstration came from Katori's group, so I treat it as part of Katori's credit, but Lemonde and SYRTE, and PTB and NIST groups on Yb and Sr, have a real secondary claim, and nobody on the committee has checked the priority record. I rely on the experts for that.

responses.point: She prefers B008 but says she would not block B025 and would move to it if the priority of the first Sr lattice-clock demonstration is confirmed.
responses.response: The chair's question on priority is the right one, and my answer is that the idea and the first demonstration both come from Katori's group (the magic-wavelength proposal and Takamoto's Sr clock), while Ye's group later took the same scheme to 10^-18. That supports your test, the original demonstration and not the most precise one, because it points to Katori and then Ye and not to a third name. I would still ask the expert reports to confirm the record, as I cannot verify the early dates myself. On B008 I find the Scherzer-limit argument strong and I respect that you disclosed your bias, but the TEM and STEM corrector claims look to me like two branches with a visible gap, and I would not hold a three-name prize that leaves out Krivanek, Dellby and Batson.

responses.point: He moved from B017 to B036 and asks whether a precision-measurement prize is better attributed than topological insulators, naming that as what would change his ranking.
responses.response: On your own test, I think B025 is better attributed: two names, a single device concept, and no predictor left outside, whereas for B036 you and Eriksson both acknowledge that Bernevig, Hughes and the late Zhang predicted the effect Molenkamp measured, and that the 3D work is also outside the trio. I accept your point that the Z2 class was not covered by the 2016 prize, and I would not call B036 unsound. But a prize that the committee has to explain by the omissions would be a harder one to defend. I cannot judge the condensed-matter details and I defer to you on whether the omissions can be answered in the citation.

responses.point: He treats Takamoto's Sr demonstration as part of Katori's own credit and Lemonde's group as a real but secondary contribution, and he discloses a mentor-lineage link to Hall and Ye.
responses.response: I agree with you on Takamoto and Lemonde, and I would handle it by drawing the citation around the lattice clock and not the clock lineage in general. On your disclosure, as chair my view is that it needs disclosure and not recusal: you spent a year in Hall's laboratory, which is a mentor-lineage connection to Ye's environment, with no collaboration, no joint funding and no stake in the outcome. I would ask you to record it in the minutes and, if the expert reports raise any new question on Ye's priority, to let colleagues lead on it. If any member thinks that is too lenient I would like to hear it before the ballot.

responses.point: She prefers B025 but asks whether the thorium work should stay out and whether the experimental priority of Katori's group against the early Sr work is settled, and she ranks the interpretation as beyond revision.
responses.response: We agree that the thorium nuclear clock stays out, and the citation I propose says lattice clocks and nothing about nuclei. On the priority question, I take it from your statement that Katori proposed and first demonstrated the scheme, so I would ask the experts to confirm that and I would not word the citation to credit Ye for the first demonstration. My earlier question about the blackbody and lattice-light-shift evaluation is still open, and you are the member best placed to judge it. If you tell us the 10^-18 claim survives that evaluation I will treat it as settled.

responses.point: He holds B003 with less confidence, says the three spokespersons are a proxy and not a demonstrated identification of who was decisive, and names B036 and B025 as fallbacks.
responses.response: I agree that the attribution is the problem. I fully accept the Higgs discovery as the most consequential result on the list, but I also do not see how three names can fairly represent two collaborations of thousands, and I do not think the committee can show that these three were decisive. You say that if the expert reports cannot support them, you would move to B025 or B036. I ask you to consider B025 first, since it shares your criterion of a clean attribution and a measured result confirmed independently. As for my own change from IceCube, I stand by it: the source picture is still too thin for a prize now.

responses.point: He ranks B036 first, saying that every member who ranked it proposed the same trio, and that a Z2 and HgTe citation keeps it distinct from 2016.
responses.response: I take B036 seriously and it remains my first alternative. Agreement on the trio shows that members propose the same names, but it does not show that the committee can defend the omission of Bernevig and Hughes, who are alive. You say that you would not stretch the prize to add names, but with a three-name limit the committee would have to choose between a prediction and an experiment, and that is the point on which I would expect external criticism. I would ask whether you consider B025 acceptable if it is the broadest common ground, as I understood from your alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether the priority record supports Katori and Ye alone, or whether Takamoto, Lemonde or the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups have a claim large enough to change the names.

Whether the committee will see a lattice clock as a measured discovery or as an enabling precision tool next to the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I have not been able to answer that with a result that is a new fact about nature.
Whether the 10^-18 evaluation (blackbody and lattice light shift) is as robust as the supporters say, which I leave to Lindroth and the expert reports.
Whether the omission of Bernevig and Hughes can be defended in the B036 case, which decides whether B036 is a real competitor.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged. I have no tie to Katori, Ye or the lattice-clock groups: my work is PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur. For B007 I work in the broad astroparticle field and Fermi-LAT contributed to TXS 0506+056 follow-up, with no personal or institutional tie to IceCube, Halzen or Spiering, and B007 is no longer my preference. On Kroll's disclosure of the Hall and Ye lineage, my judgement as chair is that disclosure in the record is enough and recusal is not needed.
